question.prompt: Let \(c\) be a real number, and let \(z_1,\) \(z_2\) be the two complex numbers satisfying the quadratic \(z^2-cz+10=0.\) Points \(z_1,\) \(z_2,\) \(\dfrac{1}{z_1},\) and \(\dfrac{1}{z_2}\) are the vertices of a (convex) quadrilateral \(Q\) in the complex plane. When the area of \(Q\) obtains its maximum value, \(c\) is the closest to which of the following?

solutions.title: Use the trapezoid coordinates
solutions.explanation:
The four vertices cannot all be real, because they would then be collinear. Thus the quadratic has nonreal roots. Since its coefficients are real, conjugating the equation shows that the roots form a conjugate pair.

Write
\[
z_1=u+vi,\qquad z_2=u-vi,\qquad v>0.
\]
The sum and product of the roots give
\[
c=2u,\qquad u^2+v^2=10.
\]
Rationalizing the reciprocals yields
\[
\frac1{z_1}=\frac{u-vi}{u^2+v^2}=\frac{u-vi}{10},
\qquad
\frac1{z_2}=\frac{u+vi}{10}.
\]
Thus the vertex coordinates are
\[
(u,v),\quad(u,-v),\quad\left(\frac{u}{10},\frac{v}{10}\right),\quad\left(\frac{u}{10},-\frac{v}{10}\right).
\]
Also, \(u\ne0\), since otherwise the vertices would lie on the imaginary axis.

The two vertical segments joining conjugate points are the parallel bases of a trapezoid. Their lengths are \(2v\) and \(v/5\), and their horizontal separation is \(9|u|/10\). Therefore its area is
\[
A_Q=\frac12\left(2v+\frac v5\right)\frac{9|u|}{10}
=\frac{99}{100}|u|v.
\]
Because \(u^2+v^2=10\), AM-GM applied to the positive numbers \(u^2\) and \(v^2\) gives
\[
|u|v=\sqrt{u^2v^2}\le\frac{u^2+v^2}{2}=5.
\]
Equality holds exactly when \(u^2=v^2=5\). Both signs of \(u\) produce valid convex trapezoids, so the maximum area is \(99/20\), attained at
\[
\boxed{c=\pm2\sqrt5}.
\]

The positive maximizer is approximately \(4.472\), closest to \(4.5\). For the negative maximizer, \(4.5\) is also the closest listed value because it is the smallest of the five positive choices. Thus both maximizing values give choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).

solutions.title: Maximize a larger triangle
solutions.explanation:
The reciprocals form a scaled copy of the original root pair. This lets us maximize the area of a triangle instead of computing the trapezoid's dimensions.

Real roots would put all four vertices on the real axis, so the roots are nonreal. Because the coefficients are real, conjugating the equation gives the other root. Write
\[
z_1=u+vi,\qquad z_2=u-vi,\qquad v>0.
\]
The root sum and product give
\[
c=2u,\qquad u^2+v^2=10.
\]
Let \(O\) be the origin, and let \(A\) and \(B\) represent \(z_1\) and \(z_2\). Then
\[
OA=OB=\sqrt{10}.
\]
Moreover, \(z_1z_2=10\) gives
\[
\frac1{z_1}=\frac{z_2}{10},\qquad
\frac1{z_2}=\frac{z_1}{10}.
\]
Let \(A'\) and \(B'\) represent \(z_1/10\) and \(z_2/10\). They lie one tenth of the way along \(OA\) and \(OB\). Since \(u\ne0\) for a nondegenerate quadrilateral, \(Q\) is exactly the trapezoid remaining when triangle \(OA'B'\) is removed from triangle \(OAB\).

The smaller triangle has linear scale factor \(1/10\), hence area scale factor \(1/100\). Thus
\[
\operatorname{Area}(Q)=\frac{99}{100}\operatorname{Area}(OAB).
\]
Using \(OA\) as a base, the altitude from \(B\) is at most \(OB\). Therefore
\[
\operatorname{Area}(OAB)\le\frac12 OA\cdot OB=5,
\]
with equality exactly when \(OA\perp OB\).

At equality, the Pythagorean theorem gives
\[
AB^2=OA^2+OB^2=20.
\]
But \(AB=2v\), so \(v^2=5\), and then \(u^2=10-v^2=5\). Both signs of \(u\) are possible. Consequently the maximum area is \(99/20\), attained when
\[
\boxed{c=2u=\pm2\sqrt5}.
\]
The positive value is about \(4.472\), closest to \(4.5\). The negative value is also closest to \(4.5\) among the listed positive choices. The answer is therefore \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
